```{python}
#| include: false
# Figures in the text come from the data the notebook cached.
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data/fred_annual.csv", index_col="year").dropna()
first, last = int(df.index[0]), int(df.index[-1])
birth = df["Birth_Rate_Per_1000"]
gdp = df["Real_GDP_Per_Capita"]
worth = df["Household_Net_Worth"] / 1e6  # trillions of nominal dollars
corr = df.corr()["Birth_Rate_Per_1000"]
```

## Overview

Do richer countries have fewer children? This project looks at one country over time: the United States from `{python} first` to `{python} last`. It sets the crude birth rate (births per 1,000 people) against two measures of national prosperity, real GDP per person and total household net worth.

## Key Findings

- **The birth rate more than halved.** It fell from `{python} f"{birth[first]:.1f}"` births per 1,000 people in `{python} first` to `{python} f"{birth[last]:.1f}"` in `{python} last`.
- **Income more than tripled.** Real GDP per person rose from \$`{python} f"{gdp[first]:,.0f}"` to \$`{python} f"{gdp[last]:,.0f}"`.
- **Wealth grew far faster.** Household net worth went from \$`{python} f"{worth[first]:.1f}"` trillion to \$`{python} f"{worth[last]:.0f}"` trillion, in nominal dollars.
- **The two move in opposite directions.** The birth rate's correlation with income is `{python} f"{corr['Real_GDP_Per_Capita']:.2f}"` and with net worth `{python} f"{corr['Household_Net_Worth']:.2f}"`.

{{< embed birth_wealth_income.ipynb#fig-birth-wealth >}}

## Reading the Numbers

- **National totals, not families.** These are country-wide figures. They say nothing about whether richer *households* have fewer children.
- **Correlation, not cause.** All three series trend over the whole period, so a strong correlation is close to guaranteed. Education, contraception, women's work, housing costs and age at marriage all moved over the same years.
- **Nominal wealth.** Net worth is not adjusted for inflation, while GDP per person is. Part of the rise in wealth is rising prices.
- **The birth-rate series starts in 1960**, so the post-war baby-boom peak is only partly shown.

## Data and Code

The data comes from FRED: the World Bank crude birth rate (SPDYNCBRTINUSA), BEA real GDP per capita (A939RX0Q048SBEA), and Federal Reserve household net worth (HNONWRA027N), averaged to calendar years. The [notebook](birth_wealth_income.ipynb) downloads and caches them.

The code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/eschnitger/eschnitger.github.io/tree/main/projects/birth-wealth-income).
